A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CM-TDP research work. Their main text, algorithms, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original pricing simulations for linear and RKHS utilities under online-to-online and offline-to-online transfer, including regret curves and quantitative transfer gains.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation results and adds dense-shift and higher-dimensional experiments, together with measured runtimes.

M1.justification: Algorithm 3 replaces logistic classification on joint price-context features with estimation of g(x) using a context-only kernel and the likelihood defined by F(p-g(x)). This substantially revises the specified RKHS estimation component. Algorithm 2 also corrects its reversed condition for whether an aggregate estimate is supplied. The outer aggregation, debiasing and episodic pricing framework remains.

E1.justification: Section 7 adds dense-difference simulated markets, allowing linear parameter differences on up to 0.5d coordinates and RKHS discrepancies up to 0.5, alongside the retained identical and sparse-difference scenarios. These extend preference-shift coverage within the same simulated pricing task and utility classes.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator remains the single-market/no-transfer learner of Javanmard and Nazerzadeh, cited as [18] in v1 and [19] in v2. Meta-DP, TLDP and MOLAR remain related-work comparisons rather than evaluated baselines. The added experiments introduce no new comparator method.

E3.justification: The dimension grid expands from {10,15,20} to include 100, and Appendix D.2.2 introduces runtime evaluation. Section 7 revises the noise specification from logistic noise supported on [-1,1] to logistic noise on R with simulated valuations clipped to [-1,1]. This is a reported protocol revision; it does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Dense-shift and d=100 experiments extend robustness and scalability testing, while Appendix D.2.2 adds systematic runtime analysis across dimensions, source-stream counts and offline sample sizes for both utility classes and transfer regimes. These substantially broaden supplementary analysis. The original sparse-shift benchmarking is retained in D.2.1 rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix C and v2 Appendix D.2.1 both report standard-error reductions across 10 Monte Carlo runs. The shaded-curve presentation is retained. No changed run count, seed protocol, confidence-interval procedure or significance test is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds dense-shift and d=100 regret curves and Table 3 runtime measurements. Every numerical entry in v1 Table 1 is retained in v2 Table 2. The new runtime discussion claims sublinear scaling with dimension, but Table 3 reports online linear runtime increasing from 77 to 972 seconds between d=10 and d=100 at K=10, contradicting that claim.

T1.justification: v2 adds linear and RKHS lower-bound Theorems 6 and 11 with proof Appendices G and J, plus computational complexity analysis. It strengthens revenue regularity, replaces covariance-smoothed RKHS discrepancies with a direct norm bound, and revises the earlier appendix smoothness condition to cover every market utility. The RKHS estimation-error and regret derivations are substantially rewritten.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the unified transfer-pricing framework, linear/RKHS minimax-optimality and novelty claims, advertised regret rates, and 50% regret-reduction and 5x learning-speed headlines. The added lower-bound statements and experiments support claims already made in v1 rather than introduce new headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for unregularized source estimation versus regularized target debiasing and for the parametric/nonparametric regret gap. Its conclusion explicitly discusses homogeneous-covariate restrictions and the absence of mechanisms to exclude adversarial sources, replacing v1's brief future-work sentence with more substantive applicability boundaries and extensions. New runtime discussion also interprets computational efficiency.

D1.justification: The code reference changes from an anonymous repository to a named GitHub repository. Appendix C newly identifies Newton's method as the implemented optimizer, and Table 3 supplies wall-clock timings. Hardware specifications and existing kernel parameters were already disclosed in v1; the new optimizer disclosure does not establish an implementation change.

R1.justification: v2 adds five references covering spectral/integral-operator learning, nonparametric estimation, batch auctions and meta-RL. It also withdraws the statement that its revenue regularity assumption is weaker than Javanmard and Nazerzadeh's. The broader positioning against Meta-DP, TLDP and multitask bandits remains, while several existing references receive publication updates.

P1.justification: The eight-section main narrative remains intact. Changes include terminology and paragraph editing, expanded estimator explanations and future work, revised notation documentation, and appendix organization into computational complexity and additional experimental results. These are limited editorial and structural revisions alongside substantial scientific additions.

P2.justification: The experimental displays are extensively reorganized: Figures 1–2 show d=10 and d=100, retained intermediate dimensions move into Figures 5–6, and offline Figures 3–4 expand from six to twelve panels. v2 also adds a two-page notation table and runtime Table 3. The original transfer-gain table is relocated and renumbered as Table 2.

improvement.justification: Corrected estimator specifications, broader stress tests, runtime measurements and explicit limitations improve clarity and empirical documentation over v1. However, the central minimax claim remains inadequately supported: Appendix J derives a packing exponent of 1/(alpha beta), although its displayed construction yields 1/(2 alpha beta). The new sublinear-runtime interpretation also conflicts with Table 3. The practical and explanatory gains therefore support a limited overall improvement.
